group: moving separators on a lattice of 10s (particle system), not solved
title: What is known about 1RB1RC_1LC0RC_0RA0LD_0LE---_0LF1LD_1LC1LE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RC_1LC0RC_0RA0LD_0LE---_0LF1LD_1LC1LE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape is a lattice of 10s cut by separators; the head bounces between the left end and the first wall (two separators side by side). Lean proves whole bounces for every list of blocks; collisions between separators are described from simulation only, and nothing yet rules out the short-block pattern that halts.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 119,943 cells have been visited and 59,948 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.515). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.069).

claims.title: 9 sweep rules, for all n
claims.text: The head crosses a run of n copies of a short word in one go, for all n and any tape around it.

claims.title: Whole bounces, for every list of blocks
claims.text: From the left end in state A to the first wall and back: with an odd number of single separators before the wall, the left block gains two 10s, odd separators move one 10 right, even ones stay, and the wall toggles 0 0 ↔ 0 1, moving one 10 right every second bounce; with an even number, a new block is written at the left end and the roles of odd and even swap. Four theorems, for every number of blocks and all lengths ≥ 3 (a seqtm sequence crossed by induction).

claims.title: The motion between collisions
claims.text: In the first 3·10<sup>8</sup> steps, every one of the 18,678 bounces without a collision moves the separators before the first wall and the wall as the bounce rules say.

claims.title: Collisions
claims.text: A moving separator that reaches the fixed one in front of it forms a new wall with it, which becomes the first wall and freezes the tape to its right; the first wall reaching the next separator merges with it into one separator, and the next wall becomes the first. Only when no wall is left does a bounce reach the right end, adding two cells there: the right side grows like a logarithm, the left side (one 10 per bounce) like a square root.

claims.title: No halt in 9.1·10<sup>40</sup> steps
claims.text: An exact accelerated simulator (the macro machine of bbtools.macro with 2-cell blocks, plus jumps over repeated periods of bounces) runs 9.1·1040 steps in 15 minutes without a halt. It agrees with the plain C simulator on the whole tape (a hash) at 106, 108, 109, 3.6·109, 2·1010 and 5·1010 steps; the jumps themselves are not proved.

claims.title: Halting needs short blocks
claims.text: Random tapes of the run's shape halt within 105 steps in about 3% of cases when the blocks have length 1 or 2 (always by the head in A meeting two 1s side by side or a similar short pattern), never in 1,600 trials with all blocks ≥ 3. Changing one block of the real tape at step 106 by one 10 gave no halt in 2·107 more steps in 40 trials.

claims.title: No halt in the first 5.60×10<sup>23</sup> steps of an accelerated run
claims.text: Observed, not proved: the accelerated simulator rsim.py ran 5.60×1023 steps from blank tape without reaching a halting transition. Its tape, state and head position were equal to those of a plain C simulator at 6 checkpoints, the last at 1.09×1010 steps. Of these steps, the part after the last checkpoint rests on the simulator alone, including 7,120 trip-level jumps: a jump applies many identical round trips at once after seeing the same tape shape recur with constant count changes, which is validated against direct simulation but not proved.

claims.title: Closed tape languages
claims.text: Windows of up to 10 cells do not close without halting (from 9 on, the right automaton takes every window). Windows of up to 6 letters (cells and runs of 10 of length 1, 2 or ≥ 3) close, but allow halts next to rows of blocks of length 1.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Next step: prove the collision rules and show that no collision produces the short-block pattern that halts.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0LB_0LC0RD_1LA1LB_0RE---_0RF1RD_1RB1RE up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The tape is a long row of 10s cut into blocks by separators. The head bounces between the left end and the first wall (two separators side by side); each bounce moves every other separator one step right, and the separators collide like particles. Lean proves the bounces for every list of blocks; whether a collision can ever make the pattern that halts is open.

facts.text: Whole bounces proved in Lean for every list of blocks.
No halt in an exact accelerated simulation.
Halting needs a block of length 1 or 2 in the wrong place.
No halt in the accelerated simulator (observed, not proved; checked against direct simulation up to 1.09×10<sup>10</sup> steps).

sections.heading: A lattice of 10s, cut by separators
html: Write a for 10. The tape is ax 0 ay 0 az …: blocks of as cut by single extra 0s, the separators, and here and there a wall, two separators side by side, written 0 0 or 0 1 by its phase. No sweep ever changes a block of as: the head crosses them whole. Only the separators move.

sections.heading: Every other separator moves
html:
The head bounces between the left end and the first wall; whatever lies past the first wall is frozen. Number the separators before the wall 1, 2, 3, … from the left. In one bounce (with an odd number of them):

whatchange per bounce
left endone a further left (the first block gains two)
odd separatorsone a to the right
even separatorsstay
first walltoggles 0 0 ↔ 0 1, one a to the right every second bounce

With an even number of separators, a new block a appears at the left end instead and odd and even swap roles. These four rules are proved in Lean for every number of blocks (lean/Bounce.lean). Example, at steps 242,652, 243,150, 243,654: blocks 3 45 38 5 17 12 | 10 become 5 44 39 4 18 12 | 9, then 7 43 40 3 19 11 | 9 (| the wall).

sections.heading: Walls are born and die
html: The block between a moving separator and the fixed one ahead of it shrinks by one a per bounce. When it is used up the two separators form a new wall, which becomes the first wall and freezes everything to its right. The first wall creeps right and, when it reaches the next separator, the three cells merge into one separator; the next wall downstream becomes the first one. Only when no wall is left does a bounce reach the right end of the tape and add two cells there, so the right side grows like a logarithm of the step count and the left side, one a per bounce, like its square root.

sections.heading: 10<sup>40</sup> steps
html: Since bounces repeat with counts that change linearly, a simulator can jump over many of them at once. py/accel.py does that on top of a run-length macro machine; it matches the plain simulator on the whole tape up to 5·1010 steps and reaches 9.1·1040 steps in 15 minutes, with no halt; by then the tape is 3.8·1020 cells wide.

sections.heading: How it would halt
html: The only halting transition is D1. D is entered from C1 and E1, both moving left, so the machine halts when one of them lands on a 1: for example the head in A meeting 1 1. That takes a block of length 1 or 2 in the wrong place. Random tapes of the same shape halt in about 3% of cases when their blocks are that short, and never when all blocks have length at least 3; in the run from blank tape short blocks appear only next to the left end and in collisions, and have never done it. Turning that into a proof needs the collision rules in Lean and an invariant on how separators are arranged.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: Separators on a lattice of 10s move like particles (half of them one cell pair per bounce, walls at half speed) and collide; whole bounces proved in Lean for every list of blocks, no halt in 9.1·10^40 steps (exact accelerated simulation); open.
